learn.title: Tidal Stream Energy: Predictable Ocean Power
learn.intro: Tidal stream energy taps into predictable ocean currents, offering reliable renewable power. With 3.7 billion people living near coasts, harnessing tidal energy can reduce fossil fuel dependence while leveraging India’s 7,600 km coastline for sustainable energy.
learn.c1_text: Tidal turbines, like underwater windmills, convert kinetic energy from flowing tides into electricity. A single turbine can generate 1-2 MW, enough to power 1,000 homes annually. Unlike solar/wind, tides operate 18+ hours daily, ensuring consistent output.
learn.c2_text: Tidal energy’s predictability stems from lunar cycles, making it more dispatchable than solar or wind. For example, the UK’s MeyGen project produces 11 MW consistently, reducing grid reliance on fossil fuels during peak demand.
learn.c3_text: India’s Andaman Sea and Gulf of Kutch show promise for tidal farms. The MNRE estimates 22 GW potential, but only 0.1 MW is currently harnessed. Policies like the National Ocean Energy Mission aim to scale this by 2030.

learn.title: Battery Management Systems: Battery Protectors
learn.intro: Battery management systems (BMS) ensure safe, efficient battery use in EVs and solar storage. They prevent overcharging, overheating, and extend battery life—critical for India’s 30% EV sales target by 2030.
learn.c1_text: A BMS monitors voltage, temperature, and state of charge across battery cells. For example, in a 48V EV battery, it balances cells to prevent a 50% capacity drop due to uneven aging.
learn.c2_text: BMS triggers cooling systems if temps exceed 45°C, avoiding thermal runaway. Tesla’s BMS reduces battery degradation by 20%, extending EV range from 350 km to 420 km over 5 years.
learn.c3_text: India’s 10 million EVs by 2025 require BMS to handle tropical heat. Startups like Log9 Materials develop BMS for 40°C+ climates, ensuring battery life exceeds 8 years despite frequent fast charging.

learn.title: Rooftop Solar & Net Metering in India
learn.intro: Rooftop solar lets households generate power, while net metering credits excess electricity to the grid. This policy drives India’s 8 GW rooftop solar target by 2026, reducing urban carbon footprints.
learn.c1_text: Net metering allows surplus rooftop solar power to offset grid bills. In Delhi, a 5 kW system can save ₹15,000/year. Excess energy is credited at the retail tariff rate, incentivizing adoption.
learn.c2_text: India’s net metering policy mandates DISCOMs to purchase excess power at tariff rates. However, delays in payment and capacity limits (e.g., 1 kW per household in some states) hinder growth.
learn.c3_text: India aims for 40 GW rooftop solar by 2030. Tamil Nadu leads with 1.2 GW installed, but only 15% of urban households participate. Subsidies and net metering reforms are critical to meet targets.

learn.title: Hydrogen Fuel Cells: Clean Vehicle Power
learn.intro: Hydrogen fuel cells generate electricity by combining hydrogen and oxygen, emitting only water. They power zero-emission vehicles, crucial for India’s goal to reduce transport emissions by 30% by 2030.
learn.c1_text: Hydrogen (H₂) reacts with oxygen (O₂) in a fuel cell, producing electricity, water, and heat. A single cell generates 0.7V; stacked cells power vehicles like the Toyota Mirai, which uses 5 kg of H₂ for 650 km range.
learn.c2_text: Fuel cells are 60% efficient, double that of internal combustion engines. However, hydrogen production via electrolysis requires 50 kWh/kg, making costs high. India’s National Hydrogen Mission targets 5 MW fuel cell vehicles by 2025.
learn.c3_text: India plans 1 GW renewable-powered electrolyzers by 2030. Startups like H2iv produce green hydrogen at ₹350/kg, aiming to cut fuel cell vehicle costs to $50,000 by 2030, supporting 10% EV market share.

learn.title: Direct Air Carbon Capture: Atmosphere Cleanup
learn.intro: Direct air capture (DAC) removes CO₂ directly from air using renewables. With India’s emissions rising 5% annually, DAC could offset 10 Gt CO₂/year by 2050, aligning with net-zero goals.
learn.c1_text: DAC systems use chemical sorbents to absorb CO₂, then release it via heat for storage. Climeworks’ plant in Iceland captures 4,000 tons/year, equivalent to 800 cars removed annually.
learn.c2_text: DAC requires 250–300 kWh/ton of CO₂. With India’s renewable growth (60 GW solar by 2024), excess energy could power DAC. Current costs: ₹10,000–15,000/ton, dropping to ₹5,000/ton by 2030 via scaling.
learn.c3_text: India’s National Carbon Market could incentivize DAC. Startups like Heiako develop low-cost sorbents. Policy support is critical: 1 Gt CO₂ removal by 2030 needs ₹5,000 crore investment, per IEA.

learn.title: Solar PV: Light to Electricity
learn.intro: Solar panels convert sunlight into electricity via the photoelectric effect. India’s 70 GW solar capacity (2024) could power 30 million homes, reducing coal use and air pollution.
learn.c1_text: Photons from sunlight knock electrons loose in silicon cells, creating current. A 1 m² panel generates 150W peak power. Germany’s 10 GW solar capacity offsets 10 million tons of CO₂ annually.
learn.c2_text: Monocrystalline panels reach 22% efficiency, converting 22% of sunlight to electricity. A 5 kW rooftop system in Delhi generates 6,000 kWh/year, meeting 40% of a household’s needs.
learn.c3_text: India added 13.5 GW solar in 2023, reaching 70 GW total. Policies like PLI Scheme 2.0 subsidize manufacturing, aiming for 280 GW by 2030. Tamil Nadu and Gujarat lead in utility-scale projects.
